title: Catching the ox
hook: fourth picture: he catches it, and it fights the rope

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third picture: birdsong, green willows, and a glimpse of the ox itself. Your line: there it is. Where did you catch a clear moment? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

What comes after a breakthrough? Stories about change usually stop at the moment of insight: the light comes on, the music swells, the credits roll. The oxherding pictures keep going. In the fourth picture the herdsman finally gets a rope around the ox. And the ox does not stand there grateful to be found. It throws its head, it bolts, it drags him toward the hills. The rope goes taut in his hands. Today: catching the ox.
screen: `A ROPE AROUND THE OX.` → `IT THROWS ITS HEAD AND BOLTS.` → `THE ROPE GOES TAUT.`

segments.voice: First, he has it. After searching, tracks and a glimpse, the herdsman now has the ox on a rope. In the language of the pictures, the thing he's been looking for is no longer out there in the grass. It's in his hands. Second, it's been wild a long time. The preface for this picture, in paraphrase, says the ox has lived so long in the wilderness that it's hard to hold. It still longs for the sweet grass. Its stubborn streak is still strong. Being caught doesn't erase the habits of all those years. That is very honest. A clear moment doesn't come with new reflexes. The old pulls are still there the next morning: the scroll, the snap at someone you love, the worry that circles at night. Third, it pulls hard. The verse describes the herdsman holding on with all his strength while the ox charges up toward the high ground or drifts off into misty valleys. The picture doesn't scold the ox. A wild ox pulls. That's what wild oxen do. The struggle isn't a sign the glimpse was fake; it's what holding on looks like at first. Fourth, so he doesn't let go. The preface says that to make the ox gentle, the herdsman will need the whip. Some readers hear that as firmness, not cruelty: steady effort and attention, returning again and again. The fourth picture is the stage of grip. Tomorrow's is the stage of patience. For today, it's enough to feel the rope and notice: it pulls.
screen: `AT LAST, THE OX ON A ROPE.` · `LONG IN THE WILD, STILL WILD.` · `IT PULLS HARD. THAT'S WHAT OXEN DO.` · `SO HE HOLDS ON.` · then, large: `IT PULLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and come to the breath. Before long, something will pull: an itch, a plan, a replayed argument, the urge to check the time. When it does, don't fight it and don't follow it. Just stay with it, the way the herdsman stays on the rope. Notice exactly where it tugs, in the hands, the chest, the jaw. Then come back to the breath. It will pull again. Stay again. That's the whole practice. The bell holds the time.
Catching the ox. The fourth oxherding picture: the herdsman gets the ox on a rope, and the ox, long wild, fights it. Today's word.
Your line: it pulls. Today, when one old habit tugs, stay with the tug for three breaths before you do anything. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Zen teachers often point to the fourth oxherding picture when students find that old habits return after a clear moment in practice, treating the struggle as a normal stage that calls for steady effort.

holding on with all his strength.

fork.reveal: the verse has him holding on with everything he has while the ox charges and wanders. the struggle is part of the path, not proof he failed.

original.note: Chinese (deniu): 'getting the ox', the name of the fourth oxherding picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: catching the ox is the happy ending.
what it means: getting hold of the ox, and finding that it's still wild and fights the rope.
what a scholar hears: the preface explains the struggle by the ox's long years in the wilderness: habit, not failure.
